glossary_terms.definition: Body Mass Index — a number calculated from your weight and height to describe weight category in general terms (underweight, normal, overweight, obese). Practical but limited: BMI can't tell muscle from fat, so it's not a health diagnosis.

Basal Metabolic Rate — the calories your body burns at complete rest, just to keep basic functions like breathing and heartbeat going. Usually estimated with the Mifflin-St Jeor formula from age, sex, height, and weight.
Total Daily Energy Expenditure — the total calories you burn in a day: your BMR plus physical activity and food digestion. This is the number that sets your daily calorie needs.
The unit of energy from food and drinks. Your body uses it for everything, from breathing to exercise. Calories are neutral — not the enemy, but worth managing.

When the calories you take in are fewer than what your body burns (TDEE). This is the basic principle of healthy weight loss — ideally a gentle deficit of around 300–500 kcal per day, not an extreme one.
When the calories you take in exceed what your body burns. It's needed if your goal is gaining weight or building muscle — still best done gradually and from nutritious food.
The nutrient that builds muscle and body tissue, and keeps you full longer than carbs or fat. Sources: eggs, chicken, fish, tofu, tempeh, and legumes.
The body's main energy source, broken down into glucose to fuel the brain and muscles. No need to avoid them entirely — pick fibrous ones like brown rice, oats, and root vegetables.
A nutrient that stores reserve energy and is also important for hormones and vitamin absorption. What needs limiting is trans fat and excess saturated fat — not all fat.
The part of plants your body doesn't digest, but which keeps you full longer and helps digestion. Found in vegetables, fruit, and whole grains.
All the chemical processes in your body that turn food into energy. Its speed is influenced by muscle mass, age, and activity — not something permanently 'broken' by a single diet.
The total muscle in your body. Muscle burns more calories than fat even at rest, so preserving muscle mass matters when losing weight.
Fat stored around the internal organs in the belly. This type is more linked to health risks than fat under the skin, and waist circumference is a simple way to monitor it.
The measurement around your belly at navel level. A cheap, easy complement to BMI: generally recommended below 90 cm for men and 80 cm for women in Asia.

A phase when your weight stops dropping even though your diet and activity haven't changed. It's normal — your body adapts — and it's usually passed by reviewing portions, activity, or simply being patient.
The pattern of repeatedly losing and regaining weight due to extreme diets that don't last. Besides being mentally exhausting, this pattern makes it harder to keep weight stable long-term.
A scale of how quickly a food raises blood sugar. Low-glycemic foods (e.g., oats, nuts) raise blood sugar more slowly and keep you full longer.
The level of glucose in the blood, the cells' main energy source. Its ups and downs are influenced by food, activity, sleep, and stress — not just sweet foods.
The amount of food you take in one meal. Managing portions — for example with a smaller plate or stopping before you're overly full — is the simplest way to control intake without strict dieting.

Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis — calories burned from everyday activity outside of exercise: walking, climbing stairs, tidying the house. Often underestimated, yet its contribution is significant.
Exercise against resistance — lifting weights, push-ups, squats — that builds and maintains muscle mass. Especially important during a calorie deficit so that what shrinks is fat, not muscle.

Exercise that gets the heart and lungs pumping: running, cycling, swimming, brisk walking. Great for stamina and burning calories, most effective when done regularly rather than occasionally but brutally.
The body's fluid sufficiency. Thirst is sometimes mistaken for hunger, so drinking enough before meals can help control portions naturally.
Eating with full attention: chewing slowly, tasting the food, and stopping when comfortably full. The opposite of eating while scrolling your phone until the plate is empty without noticing.
Healthy sleep habits: a regular sleep schedule, less screen time before bed, and a dark, cool bedroom. Lack of sleep disrupts hunger-fullness hormones and makes snacking tempting.

quizzes.description: 5 quick questions about the meaning and limits of BMI.

questions.explanation: The BMI formula is simple: weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. That's why it's practical — but also why it knows nothing about your body composition.
options: Weight and height
Weight and age
Waist circumference and height
Weight and blood fat levels

questions.explanation: The normal adult BMI range is 18.5–24.9. A value of 22.5 sits comfortably in the middle.
options: Underweight
Normal
Overweight
Obesity
questions.prompt: Which category does a BMI of 22.5 fall into for an adult?

questions.explanation: A muscular athlete can be recorded as 'overweight' despite low body fat. BMI is an initial screening tool, not a verdict.
options: The formula is too complicated for daily use
It can't distinguish muscle mass from fat
It only applies to people who are already dieting
It changes depending on meal times
questions.prompt: What is the main limitation of BMI?

questions.explanation: Children are still growing, so their BMI is read through percentiles on growth charts — adult categories don't apply as-is.
options: Use exactly the same adult categories
No need to measure until age 20
Use growth charts/percentiles matched to age and sex
Just guess from physical appearance
questions.prompt: For children and teenagers, how should BMI ideally be assessed?

questions.explanation: A BMI of 27 means overweight, but it's a starting point for evaluation (diet, activity, waist circumference), not a disease diagnosis.
options: Definitely unhealthy and must start a strict diet immediately
In the overweight category — use it as a trigger to review their lifestyle as a whole
A BMI above 25 always means obesity
No need to care since BMI is completely inaccurate
questions.prompt: What should someone with a BMI of 27 conclude?

quizzes.title: How Well Do You Understand BMI?

quizzes.description: Trivia about calories, BMR, and TDEE.

questions.explanation: A calorie is simply a unit of energy — your body needs it to breathe, think, and exercise. The only issue is the amount.
options: A harmful substance in fast food
A unit of energy the body uses for activity
A type of fat stored in the belly
A hormone that makes you hungry quickly

questions.explanation: BMR is the energy for your body's basic functions when you lie around all day doing nothing — usually estimated with the Mifflin-St Jeor formula.
options: Calories burned during intense exercise
The maximum calories you may eat per day
Calories the body burns at total rest
Metabolic speed after a big meal

questions.explanation: TDEE is the daily total: BMR plus all your activity. This is the number that sets your calorie needs.
options: TDEE is always smaller than BMR
TDEE = BMR + daily activity energy
TDEE and BMR are two names for the same thing
TDEE only applies to athletes
questions.prompt: Which statement about TDEE and BMR is correct?

questions.explanation: A gentle deficit of around 300–500 kcal per day is enough for healthy weight loss — no need to torment yourself.
options: Not eating at all for a whole day
Taking in fewer calories than your body burns
Avoiding all high-calorie foods forever
Exercising until every calorie is burned off

questions.explanation: About 7,700 kcal per kg of fat — which is why a realistic target is gradual loss of around 0.5 kg per week, not instant.
options: 3,500 kcal
5,000 kcal
7,700 kcal
10,000 kcal
questions.prompt: Roughly how much energy is stored in 1 kg of body fat?

quizzes.title: Calories & Energy

quizzes.description: Tell popular myths apart from the facts.

questions.explanation: Your body has no magic clock that turns food into fat at exactly 7 PM. Total intake across the day is what matters.
options: Fact — eating after 7 PM automatically turns into fat
Myth — what matters is total daily calories, not meal timing
Fact — metabolism stops completely during sleep
Myth — eating dinner actually burns calories
questions.prompt: Myth or fact: 'Eating dinner will definitely make you gain weight.'

questions.explanation: Sweat is how your body cools down; it's mostly water. Burned fat mostly leaves as carbon dioxide through your breath.
options: Fact — sweat is melted fat
Myth — sweat is mostly water; fat leaves through breath and metabolism
Fact — applies to all types of exercise
Myth — sweat has nothing to do with exercise at all
questions.prompt: Myth or fact: 'The more you sweat during exercise, the more fat you burn.'

questions.explanation: Your brain and muscles need glucose from carbs. Choose fibrous ones and manage portions — no need to demonize one nutrient.
options: Fact — carbs are the sole cause of weight gain
Myth — carbs are the main energy source; what matters is the type and portion
Fact — the body doesn't need carbs at all
Myth — carbs contain no calories
questions.prompt: Myth or fact: 'Carbs must be avoided entirely to lose weight.'

questions.explanation: Daily weight fluctuates with water and food. Weigh on the same schedule each week and watch the trend — that's honest data.
options: Fact — without a daily weigh-in, diets always fail
Myth — what matters is a consistent schedule and reading the trend, not daily numbers
Fact — daily weight never fluctuates
Myth — weighing is completely forbidden
questions.prompt: Myth or fact: 'Weighing yourself every day is mandatory to succeed.'

questions.explanation: Poor sleep raises the hunger hormone (ghrelin) and lowers the fullness hormone (leptin). Getting enough sleep is a legitimate part of the strategy.
options: Myth — sleep has nothing to do with body weight
Fact — lack of sleep disrupts hunger-fullness hormones and triggers snacking
Myth — staying up late actually burns more calories
Fact — lack of sleep directly adds 5 kg
questions.prompt: Myth or fact: 'Lack of sleep can interfere with weight management.'

quizzes.title: Myths vs Facts: Healthy Habits
